8	## Objective
9	
10	Add one MCP tool that restarts a named language server, so a corrupted server
11	recovers without a restart of the whole MCP session.
12	
13	## Context
14	
15	Neovim gives a user `:LspRestart`. Waythrough gives a coding agent nothing
16	like it. It restarts a server only when the process exits on its own, and it
17	stops restarting once the crash budget runs out. A server that stays alive but
18	answers from a stale index has no recovery today. The only cure is a restart
19	of the whole MCP server, which drops every other language server too.
20	
21	Waythrough cannot see that a server answers wrongly. The agent is the only
22	judge, so the recovery must be a tool the agent calls.
23	
24	## Model
25	
26	Today `Failed` is terminal: the supervisor goroutine returns, and nothing owns
27	the process any more. After the change, `Restart` re-enters `Starting` from
28	both `Ready` and `Failed`.
29	
30	Before:
31	
32	```mermaid
33	stateDiagram-v2
34	    [*] --> Starting: Start spawns the supervisor
35	    Starting --> Ready: readiness gate passes
36	    Starting --> Failed: crash budget spent
37	    Ready --> Starting: process exits, unrequested
38	    Failed --> [*]: supervisor returns, no owner left
39	```
40	
41	After:
42	
43	```mermaid
44	stateDiagram-v2
45	    [*] --> Starting: Start spawns the supervisor
46	    Starting --> Ready: readiness gate passes
47	    Starting --> Failed: crash budget spent
48	    Ready --> Starting: process exits, unrequested
49	    Ready --> Starting: Restart stops it, crash budget untouched
50	    Failed --> Starting: Restart re-supervises, crash budget cleared
51	```
52	
53	The graceful stop opens a window. The old process can still speak while the
54	new attempt starts, so every readiness signal must carry the generation that
55	produced it.
56	
57	```mermaid
58	sequenceDiagram
59	    participant Tool as restart_server
60	    participant Sup as supervisor loop
61	    participant Old as old process
62	    participant New as new process
63	
64	    Tool->>Old: shutdown, exit, kill after grace
65	    Old->>Sup: process exited
66	    Sup->>Sup: beginAttempt, generation N+1, status Starting
67	    Sup->>New: spawn, then handshake
68	    Old->>Sup: late $/progress end, generation N
69	    Note over Sup: must do nothing, or the tool reports ready too early
70	    New->>Sup: readiness gate passes, generation N+1
71	    Sup->>Tool: ready
72	```
73	
74	## Done when
75	
76	- `restart_server` exists as an MCP tool.
77	- A call on a running server returns only after the replacement passes its own
78	  readiness gate.
79	- A call on a server that already reached `Failed` does the same.
80	- A `get_definition` call that follows a restart answers from the new process.
81	- A test against `fakelsp` proves the old process ended and a new one serves.
82	- A test proves an explicit restart does not spend the crash budget.
83	- A test proves a late readiness signal from a retired attempt cannot mark the
84	  new attempt ready.
85	- A test proves a `Shutdown` that runs at the same time as a restart leaves no
86	  live subprocess behind.
87	
88	## Tasks
89	
90	- [ ] Tag readiness state with a generation, captured at spawn and carried by
91	      `client`, so `markReady`, `markFailed`, `tokenCreated` and `tokenClosed`
92	      from a retired attempt do nothing
93	- [ ] Split a graceful `stopProcess(ctx, grace)` out of
94	      `serverProcess.shutdown`, and make it return at once when the current
95	      attempt never spawned a process
96	- [ ] Keep the process-lifetime context in `Start`, and spawn every restart
97	      on it, never on the caller's context
98	- [ ] Add an instance-log flag to `fakelsp` that appends one line per process
99	      start, carrying the pid
100	- [ ] Add `Manager.Restart(ctx, name)` for a running server: stop it, let the
101	      supervisor begin a fresh attempt, then wait for the new readiness gate.
102	      The supervisor skips the crash-budget append on a requested stop, because
103	      `exits` is a local that only a new goroutine clears
104	- [ ] Re-supervise a `Failed` server on restart, with exactly one supervisor
105	      goroutine per server at every moment
106	- [ ] Put the `shuttingDown` read and the spawn decision under one lock hold,
107	      so no attempt can begin after `Shutdown` started
108	- [ ] Add the `restart_server` MCP tool, and make the unknown-server error
109	      list the configured names
110	- [ ] Update the tool list in `README.md`, and the request-flow and readiness
111	      sections in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`
112	
113	## Scope
114	
115	**In:**
116	
117	- `Manager.Restart(ctx, name)`, and the generation guard the readiness gate
118	  needs to survive it.
119	- Re-supervision of a `Failed` server, so the state that most needs a restart
120	  can take one.
121	- The `stopProcess` split, including the hang it carries today (H2 in the
122	  artifact).
123	- The `Shutdown` race that a slow graceful stop widens (H6 in the artifact).
124	- The `restart_server` MCP tool, one server name per call.
125	
126	**Off-limits:**
127	
128	- Automatic corruption detection. Waythrough cannot observe a wrong answer,
129	  and a health probe would only guess.
130	- Automatic retry of a tool call that fails during a restart. The agent asked
131	  for the restart, so it holds no other call in flight. A retry policy needs
132	  its own design.
133	- Config reload on restart. The new process starts from the same config entry
134	  the old one used.
135	- A restart of every configured server in one call.
136	- A `list_servers` tool. See Q2.
137	
138	## Questions
139	
140	- **Q1:** Does the 30-second `toolCallTimeout` cover the ready-wait after a
141	  restart?
142	  - Confirming: a restart of real `clojure-lsp` on a mid-size project reaches
143	    ready inside 30 seconds, measured.
144	  - Falsifying: it takes longer, so the tool reports "still starting" on a
145	    restart that in fact worked. The wait then needs its own option, with a
146	    longer default.
147	- **Q2:** Can an agent name the server to restart without a new listing tool?
148	  - Confirming: the agent reads a server name out of a failed tool call's
149	    error text, calls `restart_server` with that name, and the call works.
150	  - Falsifying: the agent guesses names and fails. A `list_servers` tool must
151	    then land first, in its own issue.
152	
153	## Artifacts
154	
155	- [[2026-08-15-restart-lifecycle-hazards]] — six hazards in the current
156	  lifecycle code, with line references at commit `b0a4a83`, and the shape of
157	  the generation guard. H1 blocks the seamless promise. H2 hangs `Shutdown`,
158	  and H6 orphans a subprocess. Both exist today, and an explicit restart makes
159	  both ordinary.

190	// initialize handshake and readiness tracking for each. It returns once

192	// WaitReady for that. A server that exits unexpectedly is restarted; one
193	// that exits too often is not — see WithRestartLimit.
194	func (m *Manager) Start(ctx context.Context) error {
195		m.mu.Lock()
196		defer m.mu.Unlock()
197	
198		for _, proc := range m.procs {
199			proc := proc

206	// wait for exit, and either restart or give up, until Shutdown is called or
207	// ctx is done. It is the only caller of proc.wait, so it is the only
208	// goroutine that calls exec.Cmd.Wait for this process, which Go allows only
209	// once per process.
210	func (m *Manager) runServer(ctx context.Context, proc *serverProcess) {
211		var exits []time.Time
212	
213		for attempt := 0; ; attempt++ {
214			// NewManager already gave proc its first readyCh/exitedCh, so a
215			// WaitReady call that snapshots them before this goroutine is even
216			// scheduled still observes the pair this attempt actually uses.
217			// Only a restart (attempt > 0) needs a fresh pair.
218			if attempt > 0 {

220			}

484	// signatureHelpFromProtocol converts a signature help result into the shape
485	// a coding agent reads. A server with nothing to say about the call site
486	// answers null, which is an empty result rather than a failure.
487	func signatureHelpFromProtocol(result *protocol.SignatureHelp) (SignatureHelp, error) {
488		if result == nil || len(result.Signatures) == 0 {
489			return SignatureHelp{}, nil
490		}
491	
492		active := activeSignatureIndex(result)

494			Signatures:      make([]Signature, len(result.Signatures)),
495			ActiveSignature: active,
496			ActiveParameter: activeParameterIndex(result, active),
497		}

499			labels, err := parameterLabels(signature)

512	// activeSignatureIndex reads which signature the server means. The spec
513	// defaults an omitted index, and one past the end of the server's own list,
514	// to the first signature.
515	//
516	// Precondition: result holds at least one signature, so the index it returns
517	// is always a valid one for callers to index Signatures with.
518	func activeSignatureIndex(result *protocol.SignatureHelp) int {
519		if result.ActiveSignature == nil {
520			return 0
521		}
522		index := int(*result.ActiveSignature)
523		if index < 0 || index >= len(result.Signatures) {
524			return 0
525		}
526		return index
527	}

529	// activeParameterIndex reads which parameter of the active signature the
530	// cursor is on. Since LSP 3.16 the active signature carries its own
531	// activeParameter, which takes precedence over the whole result's. Either
532	// one defaults to the first parameter when it is absent, and when it names a
533	// parameter the active signature does not hold.
534	//
535	// A server may also send an explicit null, meaning no parameter is active at
536	// all. That answer is only legal for a client that advertises
537	// noActiveParameterSupport, which Waythrough does not, so it reads as absent.
538	func activeParameterIndex(result *protocol.SignatureHelp, activeSignature int) int {
539		signature := result.Signatures[activeSignature]
540	
541		index, ok := signature.ActiveParameter.Get()
542		if !ok {
543			index, ok = result.ActiveParameter.Get()
544		}
545		if !ok || int(index) >= len(signature.Parameters) {
546			return 0
547		}
548		return int(index)
549	}

783	// syncFile tells the language server about path's current on-disk content:
784	// didOpen the first time, didChange whenever the content has moved on since
785	// the last sync. A tool call always reads disk fresh, so a coding agent's
786	// unsaved edits are invisible to Waythrough by design.
787	func (p *serverProcess) syncFile(ctx context.Context, path string) error {
788		content, err := os.ReadFile(path)
789		if err != nil {
790			return fmt.Errorf("read file: %w", err)
791		}
792		text := string(content)
793	
794		ext := filepath.Ext(path)
795		languageID, ok := p.entry.Filetypes[ext]
796		if !ok {
797			return fmt.Errorf("no languageId configured for extension %q", ext)
798		}
799	
800		p.mu.Lock()
801		server := p.server
802		prev, wasOpen := p.openFiles[path]
803		p.mu.Unlock()
804	
805		docURI := uri.File(path)
806	
807		// Each notification names itself in its error. The two share a return
808		// path but not a cause, so one shared wrap would label a failed didOpen
809		// as a didChange, and vice versa.
810		if !wasOpen {
811			err = server.DidOpen(ctx, &protocol.DidOpenTextDocumentParams{
812				TextDocument: protocol.TextDocumentItem{
813					URI:        docURI,
814					LanguageID: protocol.LanguageKind(languageID),
815					Version:    1,
816					Text:       text,
817				},
818			})
819			if err != nil {
820				return fmt.Errorf("didOpen: %w", err)
821			}
822			prev = openFile{content: text, version: 1}
823		} else if prev.content != text {
824			prev.version++
825			prev.content = text
826			err = server.DidChange(ctx, &protocol.DidChangeTextDocumentParams{
827				TextDocument: protocol.VersionedTextDocumentIdentifier{
828					TextDocumentIdentifier: protocol.TextDocumentIdentifier{URI: docURI},
829					Version:                prev.version,
830				},
831				ContentChanges: []protocol.TextDocumentContentChangeEvent{
832					&protocol.TextDocumentContentChangeWholeDocument{Text: text},
833				},
834			})
835			if err != nil {
836				return fmt.Errorf("didChange: %w", err)
837			}
838		}
839	
840		p.mu.Lock()
841		if p.openFiles == nil {
842			p.openFiles = make(map[string]openFile)
843		}
844		p.openFiles[path] = prev
845		p.mu.Unlock()
846	
847		return nil
848	}

1	# Restart lifecycle hazards in internal/lsp
2	
3	Read from `internal/lsp/manager.go` and `internal/lsp/client.go` at commit
4	`b0a4a83`. Line numbers are from that state of the code.
5	
6	The manager already restarts a server whose process exits on its own. An
7	explicit restart reuses that machinery, so it inherits every hazard below.
8	Three of these hazards exist today: H1, H2 and H6. Each one needs a narrow
9	coincidence to appear. An explicit restart makes all three ordinary.
10	
11	## H1 — a retired attempt can mark the new attempt ready
12	
13	`markReady` (manager.go:703) guards on `status != StatusStarting` only. It
14	does not ask which attempt is speaking. `beginAttempt` (manager.go:593) sets
15	the status back to `StatusStarting`. Two callers left over from the previous
16	attempt can then reach `markReady`. Each one marks the new server ready
17	before that server has indexed anything:
18	
19	- `negotiateReadiness` (spawned at manager.go:184) sleeps out
20	  `progressDebounce`, then calls `markReady` at manager.go:675.
21	- `tokenClosed` (manager.go:692) runs from the old process's jsonrpc2 reader.
22	  `client` holds the `*serverProcess` and nothing else (client.go:17), so a
23	  late `$/progress` `end` from the dying process reaches the live proc.
24	
25	A crash restart rarely hits this. The new process spawns milliseconds after
26	the old one dies, and the debounce is 250 ms. An explicit restart hits it
27	every time, because the graceful stop takes as long as the server needs to
28	answer `shutdown` and `exit`.
29	
30	The headline promise then breaks. `restart_server` reports ready. The agent's
31	next `get_definition` reaches a server that is still indexing.
32	
33	`markFailed`, `tokenCreated` and `tokenClosed` have the same blind spot.
34	
35	### Guard shape
36	
37	Give `serverProcess` a generation counter. Bump it in `beginAttempt`.
38	Capture it where each caller starts:
39	
40	| Caller | Captures the generation at |
41	| --- | --- |
42	| `negotiateReadiness` | the `go` statement in `runServer` |
43	| `client` | `protocol.NewClient` in `startProcess` (manager.go:624) |
44	
45	Then `markReady`, `markFailed`, `tokenCreated` and `tokenClosed` take the
46	generation and return without effect when it does not match. This is the
47	invariant the restart feature rests on, and it belongs in the same family as
48	the checks in [[2026-08-15-invariant-checks-and-coverage-gate]].
49	
50	## H2 — a failed spawn leaves exitedCh open forever, and shutdown blocks on it
51	
52	`startProcess` assigns `p.cmd` only after `cmd.Start()` succeeds
53	(manager.go:619-629). `runServer` calls `proc.wait()` only inside the
54	`err == nil` branch (manager.go:182-187), and `wait` is the only writer that
55	closes `exitedCh` (manager.go:743).
56	
57	Take a spawn that fails on an attempt that is not the first. Two things hold
58	after it:
59	
60	- `p.exitedCh` is the fresh channel `beginAttempt` made, and no one will ever
61	  close it.
62	- `p.cmd` still holds the previous attempt's finished `exec.Cmd`. That value
63	  is not nil.
64	
65	`shutdown` (manager.go:752) reads both. `cmd != nil`, so it does not take the
66	early return. It waits on `exited`, times out after `killGrace`, kills a
67	process that already finished, and then waits on `<-exited` at
68	manager.go:776 with no timer left. That wait never ends.
69	
70	The existing test at manager_test.go:217 covers `cmd == nil`, which is the
71	case where the command never existed at all. It does not reach this one.
72	
73	Today the path needs a binary that works once and then disappears. With an
74	explicit restart, an agent that restarts a server after a toolchain rebuild
75	walks straight into it. The graceful-stop primitive that restart needs is a
76	split of this same function, so the fix belongs to the same slice.
77	
78	## H3 — re-supervising a Failed server skips beginAttempt
79	
80	`runServer` calls `beginAttempt` only when `attempt > 0` (manager.go:178).
81	The comment explains why: `NewManager` already built the first
82	`readyCh`/`exitedCh` pair, so the first attempt must not replace it.
83	
84	A restart of a `Failed` server has no supervisor goroutine to signal, because
85	`runServer` returned after `markFailed` (manager.go:201-204). It needs a new
86	goroutine. That goroutine starts at `attempt == 0`, so it skips
87	`beginAttempt`. Three pieces of dead state survive:
88	
89	- `status == StatusFailed`, so `WaitReady` returns `failed to start`
90	  immediately, forever (manager.go:238).
91	- `readyCh`, closed by `markFailed` (manager.go:722), so no waiter can ever
92	  block on it again.
93	- `openFiles`, still holding the dead server's document versions, so
94	  `syncFile` sends `didChange` to a server that never saw a `didOpen`.
95	
96	Constraint: before any waiter observes a re-supervised server, its status is
97	`StatusStarting` and its `readyCh` is a fresh open channel. Reaching that
98	means `runServer` cannot read "first attempt ever" from `attempt == 0`.
99	
100	## H4 — the spawning context owns the child process
101	
102	`startProcess` uses `exec.CommandContext(ctx, ...)` (manager.go:608), and
103	that `ctx` comes from `Start`. `internal/cli/serve.go:57-58` passes
104	`context.Background()` on purpose, so the language servers outlive any single
105	MCP session.
106	
107	A restart arrives on an MCP tool call. The harness cancels that call's
108	context when the tool returns. A spawn on it kills the new server the moment
109	the agent gets its answer.
110	
111	The manager must keep the process-lifetime context it received in `Start`,
112	and spawn every restart on that one. The caller's context is still the right
113	context for the ready-wait timeout, and for nothing else.
114	
115	## H5 — fakelsp cannot show that the process changed
116	
117	A restart test must prove that the old process ended, and that a different
118	one now serves. `fakelsp` offers only `-crash-marker`
119	(fakelsp/main.go:38), which fires once and then stays quiet.
120	
121	An append-only instance log, one line per process start, gives a test a
122	direct reading. The test counts the lines, and compares the pid before and
123	after.
124	
125	## H6 — Shutdown can race a restart and leave an orphan process
126	
127	`Manager.Shutdown` copies the proc list (manager.go:468-472), then calls
128	`serverProcess.shutdown` on each entry. That function takes `p.mu`, sets
129	`shuttingDown`, and reads `cmd` and `exitedCh` (manager.go:753-758).
130	
131	`runServer` reads the same flag through `shutdownRequested` (manager.go:189),
132	just after `proc.wait()` returns. The flag read and the spawn that follows
133	take the lock twice, with a gap between them. A stop that lands in that gap
134	produces this order:
135	
136	1. Something stops the old process. `wait` closes generation N's `exitedCh`.
137	2. `runServer` reads `shuttingDown` as false, and loops.
138	3. `Shutdown` sets `shuttingDown`, and reads generation N's `exitedCh`, which
139	   already closed. It returns at once, and reports success.
140	4. `runServer` runs `beginAttempt` and spawns generation N+1.
141	
142	`serve` then returns while the new child runs. `exec.CommandContext` holds the
143	process-lifetime context from serve.go:58, which nothing cancels, so nothing
144	reaps that child. The subprocess outlives `waythrough serve`.
145	
146	A crash that coincides with `Shutdown` reaches this order today. The window is
147	one flag read wide. An explicit restart widens it to the whole graceful stop,
148	which lasts as long as the server needs to answer `shutdown` and `exit`.
149	
150	Constraint: one lock hold must cover both the `shuttingDown` read and the
151	decision to spawn. A `Shutdown` that starts first wins. A `Shutdown` that
152	starts second still stops the attempt that began while it ran.

39	func runServe(configPath string) error {

41		if err != nil {
42			return err
43		}
44		if err := config.Validate(cfg); err != nil {
45			return err
46		}
47	
48		absConfigPath, err := filepath.Abs(configPath)
49		if err != nil {
50			return fmt.Errorf("resolve %s: %w", configPath, err)
51		}
52		root := filepath.Dir(absConfigPath)

54		// The language-server subprocesses live for as long as serve runs, not
55		// for as long as any one MCP session does: only Shutdown below ends
56		// them, never the signal-aware context the MCP transport listens on.
57		manager := lsp.NewManager(root, cfg.LanguageServers)

1	# Architecture
2	
3	This document describes the file layout of Waythrough, and how a
4	request flows through the code. Read
5	[CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md) first for how to set up your
6	tools and check a change.
7	
8	## File layout
9	
10	| Path | Content |
11	| --- | --- |
12	| `cmd/waythrough/` | The `main` package. It only calls `cli.Execute`. |
13	| `internal/cli/` | The `waythrough` command-line interface: `init`, `validate`, and `serve`. |
14	| `internal/config/` | The `waythrough.yaml` schema, plus its `Load` and `Validate` functions. |
15	| `internal/lsp/` | Process lifecycle for each configured language server, and the LSP client that talks to it. |
16	| `internal/lsp/fakelsp/` | A small language server built only for `internal/lsp` tests. |
17	| `internal/editor/` | The MCP server. It turns each MCP tool call into an LSP request, and the LSP response back into MCP output. |
18	| `scripts/` | `check.sh`, the check script, and `install-git-hooks.sh`, the hook installer. |
19	| `.github/workflows/` | The CI workflow and the release workflow. |
20	| `.tools/` | A gitignored directory. It holds the pinned `golangci-lint` binary. |
21	| `.goreleaser.yaml` | The GoReleaser config for the release build and the Homebrew tap. |
22	| `waythrough.yaml` | An example config file, used when you run Waythrough from this repository. |
23	
24	## How a request flows
25	
26	1. A coding agent starts `waythrough serve` over stdio, as an MCP
27	   server.
28	2. `internal/cli` loads and validates `waythrough.yaml`, through
29	   `internal/config`.
30	3. `internal/cli` starts an `internal/lsp` manager. The manager
31	   starts one subprocess per configured language server, and waits
32	   for each one to become ready.
33	4. `internal/cli` builds the MCP server from `internal/editor`. This
34	   step registers the `get_definition`, `list_references`,
35	   `rename_symbol`, `signature_help`, and `get_diagnostics` tools.
36	5. The MCP server serves tool calls until the agent's session ends.
37	   `internal/editor` routes each call, by the file extension in the
38	   call, to the language server that handles it. It sends the LSP
39	   request through the `internal/lsp` manager, and it turns the LSP
40	   response into the tool's output shape.
41	6. When `serve` exits, it shuts down every language server the
42	   manager started.
43	
44	## Readiness
45	
46	An LSP server's process can start before the server can answer a
47	request. `internal/lsp` gates on one of two readiness signals, set
48	per server in `waythrough.yaml`:
49	
50	- `progress` — the default. The manager waits for every LSP
51	  `workDoneProgress` token the server opens to close.
52	- `handshake` — an opt-in for a server with no background indexing.
53	  The manager treats the server as ready as soon as the
54	  initialize and initialized handshake completes.
55	
56	## Add a language server
57	
58	Add an entry to `waythrough.yaml`. You need no code change. See the
59	`language_servers` schema in `internal/config/config.go`.
60	
61	## Add an MCP tool
62	
63	Add the tool to `internal/editor/editor.go`, and add the LSP call it
64	needs to `internal/lsp/manager.go`. Add tests at both levels: an
65	`internal/lsp` test against `fakelsp`, and an `internal/editor` test
66	for the tool's input and output shape.

1	# Waythrough
2	
3	A coding agent without a language server guesses at your code. It reads
4	text and looks for matching names. It does not know a symbol's
5	definition, and it does not know every place that uses it.
6	
7	Waythrough closes that gap. Waythrough is a Model Context Protocol
8	(MCP) server. It starts and manages Language Server Protocol (LSP)
9	servers. It offers their features to the agent as MCP tools.
10	
11	Point a coding agent at Waythrough. Claude Code, Codex, and
12	Antigravity are coding agents. Waythrough gives the agent the same
13	"go to definition" and "find references" power as a modern editor.
14	
15	## Status
16	
17	This project is in early setup. It has five MCP tools. Tests run
18	them against a test language server, not against a real one yet.
19	
20	## Install
21	
22	Waythrough publishes binaries for Linux and macOS. This project is
23	also its own Homebrew tap. Run these commands to install it:
24	
25	```sh
26	brew tap gustavofsantos/waythrough https://github.com/gustavofsantos/waythrough
27	brew install waythrough
28	```
29	
30	## Quick start
31	
32	1. Create a `waythrough.yaml` file in your project root. Each entry
33	   names a language server, the command that starts it, and the file
34	   extensions it handles:
35	
36	   ```yaml
37	   language_servers:
38	     - name: gopls
39	       command: gopls
40	       args: []
41	       filetypes:
42	         .go: go
43	   ```
44	
45	   Run `waythrough init` to write a starter config for Clojure
46	   instead. Edit it for your own language servers. Then run
47	   `waythrough validate` to check the file for errors.
48	
49	2. Add Waythrough as an MCP server in your coding agent's config.
50	   Pass an absolute path to `--config`, so Waythrough finds
51	   `waythrough.yaml` no matter where the agent starts it from. The
52	   agent starts Waythrough over stdio:
53	
54	   ```json
55	   {
56	     "mcpServers": {
57	       "waythrough": {
58	         "command": "waythrough",
59	         "args": ["serve", "--config", "/absolute/path/to/waythrough.yaml"]
60	       }
61	     }
62	   }
63	   ```
64	
65	3. Ask your coding agent to find a definition or list references. The
66	   agent calls Waythrough's MCP tools. Waythrough forwards the
67	   request to the language server for that file type.
68	
69	## Tools
70	
71	Waythrough exposes these MCP tools to a connected coding agent:
72	
73	- `get_definition` — find where a symbol's definition is, given a
74	  file position.
75	- `list_references` — find every place that uses a symbol, given a
76	  file position.
77	- `rename_symbol` — build the list of edits that rename a symbol,
78	  across every file it touches. It does not write the edits to disk.
79	  Your agent applies them.
80	- `signature_help` — list the signatures a call could match, given a
81	  file position inside that call. It also says which signature and
82	  which parameter the position is on.
83	- `get_diagnostics` — list the problems a language server finds in a
84	  file. The language server must advertise pull diagnostics at its
85	  handshake. One that does not fails the call with an error naming it,
86	  rather than reporting a clean file. `gopls` pushes its diagnostics
87	  by default and advertises no pull support, so it fails this call
88	  today.
89	
90	## Learn more
91	
92	- [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) — set up your tools, run the
93	  checks, and submit a change.
94	- [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) — the file layout
95	  and how a request flows through the code.
96	- [LICENSE](LICENSE) — the license for Waythrough.

# Validation gate for waythrough: formatting, vet, lint, build, module
# tidiness, and tests. This is the single source of truth run by both the
# local pre-commit hook (scripts/install-git-hooks.sh) and CI
# (.github/workflows/ci.yml) so the two never disagree.
set -uo pipefail

REPO_ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null)" || {
	echo "not a git repository" >&2
	exit 1
}
cd "$REPO_ROOT"

# Keep this in sync with .github/workflows/ci.yml.
GOLANGCI_LINT_VERSION="v2.6.2"
TOOLS_BIN="$REPO_ROOT/.tools/bin"
GOLANGCI_LINT="$TOOLS_BIN/golangci-lint"

if [ -t 1 ]; then
	RED=$'\033[0;31m'; GREEN=$'\033[0;32m'; YELLOW=$'\033[0;33m'; BOLD=$'\033[1m'; NC=$'\033[0m'
else
	RED=""; GREEN=""; YELLOW=""; BOLD=""; NC=""
fi

failures=()

pass() { printf '%s✓%s %s\n' "$GREEN" "$NC" "$1"; }
fail() { printf '%s✗%s %s\n' "$RED" "$NC" "$1"; failures+=("$1"); }

# Installs a pinned golangci-lint into a repo-local, gitignored bin dir
# rather than requiring it on $PATH, so local runs and CI use the exact
# same binary and never drift.
ensure_golangci_lint() {
	if [ -x "$GOLANGCI_LINT" ] && "$GOLANGCI_LINT" version 2>/dev/null | grep -q "${GOLANGCI_LINT_VERSION#v}"; then
		return 0
	fi
	echo "${YELLOW}Installing golangci-lint ${GOLANGCI_LINT_VERSION} into ${TOOLS_BIN}...${NC}" >&2
	mkdir -p "$TOOLS_BIN"
	if ! GOBIN="$TOOLS_BIN" go install "github.com/golangci/golangci-lint/v2/cmd/golangci-lint@${GOLANGCI_LINT_VERSION}"; then
		return 1
	fi
}

echo "${BOLD}Running validation checks in ${REPO_ROOT}${NC}"
echo

# 1. Formatting
unformatted="$(gofmt -l . 2>&1)"
if [ -n "$unformatted" ]; then
	echo "$unformatted"
	fail "gofmt (run: gofmt -w .)"
else
	pass "gofmt"
fi

# 2. Vet
if vet_out="$(go vet ./... 2>&1)"; then
	pass "go vet"
else
	echo "$vet_out"
	fail "go vet"
fi

# 3. Lint
if ensure_golangci_lint; then
	if lint_out="$("$GOLANGCI_LINT" run ./... 2>&1)"; then
		pass "golangci-lint"
	else
		echo "$lint_out"
		fail "golangci-lint"
	fi
else
	fail "golangci-lint (could not install ${GOLANGCI_LINT_VERSION})"
fi

# 4. Build
if build_out="$(go build ./... 2>&1)"; then
	pass "go build"
else
	echo "$build_out"
	fail "go build"
fi

# 5. Module tidiness
if tidy_out="$(go mod tidy -diff 2>&1)"; then
	pass "go mod tidy"
else
	echo "$tidy_out"
	fail "go mod tidy (run: go mod tidy)"
fi

# 6. Tests
if test_out="$(go test ./... -race -count=1 2>&1)"; then
	echo "$test_out"
	pass "go test"
else
	echo "$test_out"
	fail "go test"
fi

echo
if [ "${#failures[@]}" -eq 0 ]; then
	echo "${GREEN}${BOLD}All checks passed.${NC}"
	exit 0
fi

done

# Contributing to Waythrough

Thank you for your interest in Waythrough. This project is in early
setup, so expect the tool set and the config schema to change. This
guide covers how to set up your tools, check a change, and submit it.

See [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) for the file layout
and how a request flows through the code.

## Set up your tools

You need Go, at the version in [go.mod](go.mod), and git. Clone the
repository, then run this command once:

```sh
./scripts/install-git-hooks.sh
```

This command installs `scripts/check.sh` as a pre-commit hook and a
pre-push hook. Git does not track the `.git/hooks` directory, so each
clone needs this step. The pre-push hook runs on every push,
including a release tag push, so a broken release never reaches
GitHub Actions.

Both hooks check your full working tree. They do not check only the
staged or the pushed commits. An uncommitted change to a tracked file
can change the result.

If GitButler manages your `pre-commit` hook, the installer detects
this and installs to `pre-commit-user` instead. It does not overwrite
GitButler's hook.

## Build

```sh
go build ./...
```

# Way of refactoring — flock after green, commit separately

After an agent turn that makes tests **green**, do **not** fold structural cleanup into the behavior change. Commit the behavior first, then refactor under a closed scope, then land a separate `refactor:` commit.

## Gate (all required)

1. Relevant tests are green.
2. The behavior (or slice) change is **already committed** on the branch.
3. Working tree is clean except for the intentional refactor edits you are about to make.
4. User has not asked to skip refactoring or to stop after the behavior commit.

If the behavior is not committed yet: commit it first, then start this pass.

## Flocking Rules

Repeat until the next difference is no longer worth removing, or would invent a speculative abstraction:

1. **Select the things that are most alike.**
2. **Find the smallest difference between them.**
3. **Make the simplest change that will remove that difference.**

Structures and names should **emerge** from removing differences — do not design the abstraction up front and rearrange code to fit it.

## Closed scope

- Prefer alike things **inside the files / paths touched by the just-committed change** (and their direct callers/callees if needed to complete one flocking step).
- Do not open a repo-wide cleanup, rename campaign, or unrelated module rewrite.
- Do not change behavior, public contracts, or tests' asserted outcomes — only shape. If a test must change, you left the refactor lane. Stop and treat it as a new behavior turn.
- Keep tests green after every flocking step. If red, revert the step and pick a smaller difference.

## Commit

When the flocking pass is done (or the user stops you):

- Commit **only** the refactor diff.
- Message type **`refactor:`** (Conventional Commits). If a Jira key is known from the branch / change, use `refactor(<JIRA>): …`.
- Do **not** amend the prior behavior commit. Do **not** mix feat/fix/test edits into the refactor commit.

## Avoid

- Refactoring while still red, or before the behavior commit exists.
- “While I’m here” drive-bys outside the alike set.
- Introducing a new name/type “for clarity” before two concrete alike sites forced it (see also spend / vertical-slice bias).
- A single giant rewrite instead of repeated smallest-difference steps.

A restart passes the same gate. The manager stops the old process,
starts a new one, and reports ready only when that new process
passes the gate itself.

Each start of a process is one attempt, and the manager numbers
them. A stopped process can still send messages while its
replacement starts, so every readiness signal carries the attempt
that produced it. The manager drops a signal from an attempt it has
already replaced. Without this, a message from the stopped process
would report the replacement ready before that server had indexed
anything.

## Server lifecycle

One goroutine owns each language server, from `Start` to shutdown.
It starts the process, runs the handshake, and waits for the
process to exit. Then it starts another process, unless the server
has exited more often than the restart limit allows. A server in
that state waits for a restart. It does not release its goroutine,
so exactly one goroutine owns each server at all times.

This has two results. Every process starts on the context `Start`
received, so no single tool call can end a language server when
that call returns. And a restart of a server that gave up needs no
new goroutine.
